meta.note: The functional phrase inventory: WHAT a speaker or writer is doing, independent of genre. Transcribed from the classroom grids rather than derived from any pipeline, because these functions are not email-specific — advice, opinion, agreeing, preference and comparing serve Speaking Parts 2-4 at least as much as they serve letters. Email, Speaking and the site-level Phrase Bank should all FILTER this one file rather than keep private copies; the formal/informal split in emails-phrases.json drifted apart precisely because it was duplicated. Register is a property of each phrase, not a branch of the tree, so the same function can be shown across registers side by side — which is the contrast worth teaching.
meta.source: FCE writing portfolio structure 2026, function grids
meta.reviewFlags: Entries with a `convention` note carry a UK-usage contrast aimed at Portuguese L1 learners. These are drafted for the teacher to confirm, amend or delete — they are the least certain part of this file.

social.label: Social moves
social.note: Opening and sustaining the relationship. Heavily conventionalised; the place where L1 transfer shows first.

interpersonal.label: Asking & responding
interpersonal.note: Adjacency pairs — an invitation expects an acceptance or a refusal.

stance.label: Stance & attitude
stance.note: Positioning yourself towards an idea. Shared with Speaking Part 4.

advisory.label: Advice & suggestion
advisory.note: The core of the 'giving advice to a friend' letter and of Speaking Part 3 collaboration.

planning.label: Plans & arrangements
planning.note: Future forms carry the meaning here — present continuous for arrangements, going to for intentions.

comparison.label: Comparing
comparison.note: Grammar-bearing: comparative structures are examined in Use of English as well.

thanking.label: Thanking

phrases.t: Thank you very much for your help.
I'm most grateful for all you've done.
It was so kind of you to write to me.
I really appreciate your concern.
Thanks a lot for

thanking.convention: English thanks are short and land early. A Portuguese learner often postpones the thanks to the closing, or expands it; UK convention puts it in the opening line and moves on.

apologising.label: Apologising

phrases.t: I'm very sorry for not writing before.
I apologise for not sending it.
Accept my apologies for being late.
I'm afraid I've broken it.
Sorry I didn't reply sooner

apologising.convention: "I'm afraid" is an apology marker in English, not an expression of fear. It softens bad news and has no direct Portuguese equivalent.

enthusiasm.label: Showing enthusiasm

phrases.t: It was lovely to hear from you.
What a lovely surprise!
How wonderful to know that
I just can't believe that
I'm so glad that

enthusiasm.convention: Reacting to the reader's news before your own business is close to obligatory in an English informal letter. Omitting it reads as cold, and it is the move Communicative Achievement most often rewards.

phrases.t: What have you got to lose?
Keep up the good work!
You are on the right track.
That's a real improvement.

invitation.label: Inviting

phrases.t: Would you like to stay at my place?
Would you be interested in visiting us?
How about going out on that day?
Do you want to borrow mine?
I wonder if you would like to take ours.

invitation.convention: English invitations are phrased as questions about the reader's wishes, not as statements of the writer's. "I invite you to" is unidiomatic.

offering.label: Offering

phrases.t: If you like, I can give you a lift.
Would you like me to pick you up?
Shall I send it to you again?
How about lunch on that day?

offering.convention: "Shall I…?" is the standard offer form and has no Portuguese parallel; learners reach for "Do you want that I…".

phrases.t: I'd love to.
That would be lovely.
I really look forward to it.
I just can't wait.

refusing.label: Refusing

phrases.t: I'm afraid I can't.
I'm sorry, I just can't.
It won't be possible.
I have to turn it down.

refusing.convention: An English refusal opens with the softener and gives the reason after. Leading with the reason sounds like an excuse.

phrases.t: Do you think it would be all right to
What would you say if I
Are you in favour of
Would you approve of
I think this is the best solution.
I believe he is the right person.
In my opinion, this is ideal.
It seems that she was wrong.
From my point of view, this won't last.

agreeing.label: Agreeing

phrases.t: It is a great idea.
I think you're absolutely right.
I can see your point.
I agree with you 100 percent.
I couldn't agree with you more.
That's exactly how I feel.

agreeing.convention: "I couldn't agree with you more" is strong agreement, not disagreement. The negative form regularly misleads learners.

disagreeing.label: Disagreeing

phrases.t: I don't think so.
I'm afraid I disagree.
I totally disagree.
I'd say the exact opposite.
Not necessarily.
That's not always the case.

disagreeing.convention: Direct disagreement is hedged in English far more than in Portuguese. "I'm afraid I disagree" is the safe default in writing.

phrases.t: I get mad when she is late.
What annoys me is her hair.
I find her very interesting.
If there is one thing I hate, it's smoking.

preference.label: Preference

phrases.t: I would rather stay with you.
I wouldn't mind going by bus.
I'd rather you stayed with us.
It doesn't matter if it rains.
I prefer yellow to red.

preference.convention: "I'd rather you stayed" takes a past form for a present meaning — a structure with no Portuguese equivalent and a recurring Use of English item.

phrases.t: I really like swimming.
I absolutely love going out.
I really enjoy travelling.
I am keen on dancing.
I absolutely adore painting.
I really dislike ironing.
I absolutely hate dancing.
I really detest working.
I am not keen on driving.
I can't stand jazz.

advice.label: Giving advice

phrases.t: You should see a doctor.
If I were you, I wouldn't buy it.
You shouldn't eat sugar.
You ought to take it seriously.
I would advise you to accept it.

advice.convention: Advice to a friend uses second person freely in English. Learners often over-hedge into the impersonal, which weakens the letter.

suggestion.label: Suggesting

phrases.t: It might be a good idea to buy it.
Why don't you contact the manager?
You could always come with us.
We should send it back.
You had better let him know.

suggestion.convention: "You had better" carries a warning, not a mild suggestion — stronger than learners usually intend.

requesting_information.label: Requesting information

phrases.t: I would be grateful if you could
I would also like to have
I wonder if you could send me
Could you kindly send me
I am also interested in

requesting_information.convention: English politeness sits in the modal — could, would, I wonder if — not in the form of address. A Portuguese learner may open very formally and then make a bare request, which reads as brusque.

phrases.t: Well, the reason why I
It's because
This is due to the fact that
Well, considering that
The main reason is that
Firstly, one of the things that
Secondly, another thing that
What's more, one other thing
Finally, the last thing that
It is likely that he won't marry her.
It is unlikely that she will leave him.
There is no chance of them coming here.
I wouldn't be surprised if she bought it.

ability.label: Ability

phrases.t: I wasn't able to finish it.
I couldn't contact them.
I just can't understand it.
He succeeded in changing it.
He managed to get a new one.

ability.convention: "Managed to" and "succeeded in" both mean achievement against difficulty, and take different structures — to-infinitive against -ing.

phrases.t: I am planning to visit Lisbon.
I'm going to sell my flat.
I'm thinking of going tonight.
I would like to visit my family.

making_arrangements.label: Making arrangements

phrases.t: I am arriving in Lisbon at 4.
I am staying at a hotel.
I have arranged to meet my colleagues.
We are flying to Glasgow on the 3rd.

making_arrangements.convention: Fixed arrangements take the present continuous in English, where Portuguese would use a future. "I will arrive at 4" is not wrong but sounds less settled.

phrases.t: I hope it'll be sunny.
Hopefully, I won't need it.
Let's hope I can finish it.
If we're lucky, it won't rain.
He is as tall as Peter.
He plays better than I do.
The more he eats, the fatter he will be.
No one plays it as well as he does.

similarities_differences.label: Similarities & differences

phrases.t: Both of them were similar.
Neither of them was very different.
Either you get this one or that one.
Each one looks different.

similarities_differences.convention: Both / neither / either / each govern singular and plural agreement differently — a frequent Use of English item as well as a writing error.
